questions.prompt: What are friend signals in this chapter?
choices: Low-threat nonverbal cues that make another person more willing to stay in the interaction
Private thoughts that help you feel confident before speaking
Persuasion tactics used after trust is already established

explanation.gentle: The chapter uses friend signals to describe nonverbal cues that communicate safety and approachability.
explanation.direct: Friend signals are early low-threat indicators, not internal thoughts or late-stage tactics.
explanation.competitive: They are gate-opening cues, not hidden confidence tricks.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat first impressions as so important?
choices: Because one cue guarantees permanent trust
Because early nonverbal reads can shape whether a person keeps engaging
Because words are mostly irrelevant in relationships

explanation.gentle: The chapter says early impressions matter because they influence whether the other person keeps giving the interaction time.
explanation.direct: First impressions shape future opportunity, not because they are final, but because they affect whether contact continues.
explanation.competitive: They matter because they decide who gets runway and who gets cut off early.

questions.prompt: Which set of cues best matches the chapter's main examples of friend signals?
choices: Eyebrow flash, head tilt, smile, and open posture
Fast speech, louder volume, direct staring, and sharp gestures
Long explanations, persuasive stories, and frequent compliments

explanation.gentle: Those are the chapter's main examples of low-threat opening cues.
explanation.direct: Schafer centers eyebrow flash, head tilt, smile, and open posture rather than forceful verbal tactics.
explanation.competitive: Option A names the actual gate-opening signals.

questions.prompt: Jonah is about to enter a small networking group. Which move best fits the chapter?
choices: Lead with a low-threat entry through open posture and a warm facial read before pushing content
Interrupt quickly with strong facts so the group sees his confidence
Stay visibly guarded until someone proves they are worth talking to

explanation.gentle: The chapter's advice is to lower threat first so the interaction has a chance to continue comfortably.
explanation.direct: Jonah's first job is approachability, not dominance or defensiveness.
explanation.competitive: Win the runway before you try to win the room.

questions.prompt: A professor seems cold right after Nia begins her presentation, even though her content is solid. What does the chapter suggest she review first?
choices: Whether her opening nonverbal cues raised threat before the argument had time to help
Whether the topic was impossible for any student to explain well
Whether she should ignore body language entirely and only improve her slides

explanation.gentle: The chapter pushes the reader to inspect the first emotional read, not only the script.
explanation.direct: Nia may have created a chilly opening through her early cues even if her ideas were sound.
explanation.competitive: The gate may have failed before the content even got its shot.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's strongest warning about a negative first impression?
choices: It is impossible to recover from under any circumstances
It can reduce future contact, which makes later repair and closeness harder
It matters only in formal work settings

explanation.gentle: The chapter does not say recovery is impossible. It says a bad opening reduces the chance to earn more time.
explanation.direct: Negative first impressions hurt because they shrink relationship runway.
explanation.competitive: A bad first read does not just sting. It cuts off future reps.

questions.prompt: A friend greets people with the right smile and posture but then acts cold and self-focused. How would this chapter read that pattern?
choices: The opening signals still guarantee a strong bond
The friend signals helped too much, so later behavior no longer matters
The early cues may open the door, but the advantage fades when later behavior contradicts them

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the opening cues help only if later behavior supports them.
explanation.direct: Friend signals are not trust; they are invitations that collapse when the follow-through feels false.
explanation.competitive: A good first minute cannot carry a fake next ten.

questions.prompt: Mateo knows he landed badly in his first office-hours meeting. What fits the chapter best for the second try?
choices: Raise the intensity immediately so the professor has to take him seriously
Re-enter with lower-threat cues instead of more force, then make the point clearly
Avoid the professor forever because first impressions are final

explanation.gentle: The chapter treats repair as harder after a bad opening, but not impossible if the second entry lowers threat.
explanation.direct: Mateo should avoid reinforcing the first negative read and instead create a safer opening.
explanation.competitive: He does not need more edge. He needs a cheaper re-entry.

questions.prompt: What deeper tension does the chapter leave open about deliberate signaling?
choices: Whether thoughtful cue control can slide into empty performance if later behavior does not match
Whether body language matters more than every other part of a relationship forever
Whether friend signals should be kept secret from everyone

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps a real line in view between considerate signaling and behavior that starts to feel engineered.
explanation.direct: Deliberate cue control is useful, but it becomes shallow when it is not backed by genuine follow-through.
explanation.competitive: The live question is where social intelligence turns into stagecraft.

questions.prompt: Why does this chapter naturally lead into a chapter about making people feel good about themselves?
choices: Because once the opening threat is lowered, the next job is to make the interaction rewarding, not just safe
Because first impressions make all later behavior unnecessary
Because friend signals only work after a long relationship already exists

explanation.gentle: The opening signal helps someone stay, but the next step is giving them a reason to enjoy the interaction itself.
explanation.direct: Chapter 3 follows because approachability opens contact, while real liking depends on how the exchange feels afterward.
explanation.competitive: Access is the start. Enjoyment is what keeps the person coming back.
